title: The Quiet Rise of the Biryani Belt: How One Franchise Built 50 Outposts Across America
excerpt: Bawarchi Biryanis, run almost entirely by Telugu-American families, has become the largest Indian restaurant franchise in the US — and just opened inside a Colorado hotel.
body:
In the parking lot of a Hilton Garden Inn in Fort Collins, Colorado, something improbable has happened. Between the continental breakfast station and The Garden Grille and Bar, a Hyderabadi biryani franchise has set up shop — and the locals are lining up for it.

Bawarchi Biryanis, the Telugu-diaspora-built franchise that now operates more than 50 locations across the United States, opened its newest outpost inside the hotel this week. Owned by Saiprasad and Sunita Palusa, the Fort Collins expansion is a second location for the couple, who have run the original Bawarchi on South College Avenue for more than a decade, with the Swagath Indian grocery store right next door.

"I wanted to bring more community to the Harmony area and introduce more diners to South Indian cuisine," Sunita Palusa told the Fort Collins Coloradoan. She will operate the hotel location while her husband continues to run the original.

## The Biryani Franchise Model

If the momo is having its moment and dosa has its devotees, biryani has quietly become the most franchisable Indian dish in America. Bawarchi Biryanis — whose name means "chef" in Urdu — has grown from a single outpost into a national chain with locations stretching from Newark, Delaware, to Sanford, Florida, to Aurora, Illinois, to the Bay Area. Its owners, Kishore Kancharla and Ramanaidu Suryadevara, claim the franchise serves close to a million customers monthly.

The model is simple but effective: offer more than 30 varieties of biryani (from Avakai to Military to Gongura Goat), keep prices accessible, and rely on local Telugu-American families to own and operate each location. Unlike the Michelin-chasing fine-dining restaurants that draw magazine covers, Bawarchi operates in strip malls, near Indian grocery stores, and now apparently inside hotel lobbies. It is the Subway of Indian food — and that is not an insult.

## A Telugu-American Story

Bawarchi's expansion is inseparable from the Telugu diaspora itself. The franchise's customer base and ownership pool overlap almost entirely with the Telugu-speaking community that has grown rapidly across America's tech corridors — from the Bay Area and Seattle to Dallas, Atlanta, and New Jersey. The franchise's press releases are distributed through Telugu media outlets. Its grand openings feature Tollywood-adjacent fanfare.

This is a distinctly different path from the high-profile Indian restaurant empires built by chefs like Sujan Sarkar or Vikas Khanna. There are no Michelin aspirations, no cocktail programs with vetiver and kokum. Instead, there is a mother who recognized that the Indian families moving to Fort Collins's Harmony corridor wanted the same biryani they left behind in Hyderabad — and decided to give it to them inside a Hilton.

The Sanford, Florida, location followed a similar arc: owner Rekha Nidadavolu soft-launched a fast-casual takeout operation, with plans to expand to 40 seats as city permits come through. In Naperville, Illinois, a new branch joined the existing Schaumburg location, with Buffalo Grove on deck. Each new outpost follows the same template: local Telugu-American owner, familiar menu, rapid community adoption.

## Biryani's Crossover

Biryani's appeal has always been broader than its immigrant base. The dish — fragrant, layered, satisfying in a way that transcends cultural literacy — needs no explanation. It works as a $12 lunch and a $25 dinner. It travels well for delivery and catering, which Bawarchi has leveraged to cater events of up to 15,000 people at national conventions.

What Bawarchi has done, without attracting the food-media spotlight, is prove that Indian cuisine can scale in America the same way Chinese, Thai, and Mexican food did — through affordable, consistent, community-rooted franchise operations. While the food press celebrates tasting menus, the biryani belt is being built one hotel lobby and one strip mall at a time.

## What's Next

Bawarchi has announced upcoming locations in Tampa, Jacksonville, Los Angeles, and additional Bay Area outposts. The Fort Collins hotel model could prove especially interesting: Indian restaurants inside American hotels represents a new frontier for the franchise, one that introduces biryani to travelers who might never walk into a standalone Indian restaurant.

For Sunita Palusa, the bet is straightforward. She has watched her husband build a loyal clientele at the original Fort Collins location for a decade. Now she is expanding their bet — one plate of dum biryani at a time. Diners at the new Hilton Garden Inn location can enjoy 15 percent off through June 30.
